questions.q: A `@Scheduled` job runs in a service deployed on three instances. What happens by default?
o: It runs on all three instances at the same time
Spring elects one instance to run it each time
Only the first instance to start will ever run it
It does not run at all when deployed in a cluster
questions.w: Each JVM has its own scheduler, so the job fires on every instance. You need a lock or a central scheduler to run it once.

questions.q: Which approach makes a scheduled job run on only one instance per tick?
o: A distributed lock such as ShedLock, or Quartz clustering
A larger thread pool for the scheduler
Switching from `cron` to `fixedRate` timing
Marking the scheduled method `synchronized`
questions.w: `synchronized` only works inside one JVM. A shared lock (database row, Redis key) coordinates across instances.

questions.q: A lock holder crashes without releasing the lock. How do distributed locks avoid blocking the job forever?
o: The lock has a lease or TTL and expires on its own
Another instance forcibly kills the holder process
The lock is never held for longer than a millisecond
The database drops the lock table after a minute
questions.w: Locks use `lockAtMostFor` (ShedLock) or a Redis TTL. Set it longer than the normal job duration but short enough to recover.

questions.q: A job holds a lock with a 30-second lease but occasionally runs 45 seconds. What is the risk?
o: The lease expires and a second instance starts the same job
The database cancels the long-running job
The lock silently becomes permanent
Nothing, because the lock extends itself
questions.w: Make the job idempotent and either extend the lease while running or use a fencing token so a stale holder cannot do damage.

questions.q: Why should scheduled jobs be idempotent?
o: Jobs can run twice or be retried, and the result must stay correct
Idempotent jobs always execute faster than others
Cron expressions require idempotent code to parse
It avoids the need for a database altogether
questions.w: At-least-once execution is the realistic guarantee. Use a unique business key or processed marker so a rerun does no extra harm.

questions.q: What is the difference between `fixedRate` and `fixedDelay` in Spring?
o: `fixedRate` counts from each start, `fixedDelay` from the previous end
`fixedRate` is only valid when written as a cron-style string
`fixedDelay` runs several jobs in parallel threads by default
They behave identically in every situation that you meet
questions.w: Use `fixedDelay` when runs must not overlap in time. `fixedRate` can queue up or overlap if a run is slow.

questions.q: A nightly batch has 10 million rows to process. What scales best across instances?
o: Split the work into partitions that workers claim independently
Let one instance do everything while the others idle
Run the same full job on every instance at once
Process one row per minute to stay safe
questions.w: Partitioning (by id range or hash) lets instances share the load. Claim rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or a status column.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of a dedicated scheduler service (for example Quartz cluster or a workflow engine) over per-service `@Scheduled`?
o: Central persistence, misfire handling and a visible job history
No configuration is needed at all
Retries are no longer necessary
Jobs automatically run exactly once without any extra care
questions.w: Persistent job stores let jobs survive restarts and let you inspect, pause and retrigger them. Exactly-once still needs idempotent job code.
